newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GERMAN PROSECUTORS WANT TOUGH SENTENCE ON GRAF.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GERMAN PROSECUTORS WANT TOUGH SENTENCE ON GRAF.

text.p: German prosecutors asked a court on Tuesday to jail the father of women's world tennis number one Steffi Graf for six years and nine months for tax evasion.

Federal prosecutor Gabriele Schoepf told the Mannheim court in her closing remarks that Peter Graf, 58, had tried to evade 19.2 million marks ($12.19 million) in tax on the tennis star's earnings between 1989 and 1993.
Schoepf also asked the court to send Graf's former tax adviser Joachim Eckardt, 49, to prison for four years and nine months.

Much of what the German media has dubbed "the missing millions" was siphoned off through bank accounts in Liechtenstein, the Netherlands and on the Dutch Antilles islands in the Caribbean, prosecutors said.
Graf and Eckardt had turned their noses up at any chance to come clean, prosecutors said, as they explained why they were demanding such tough sentences.
Chief prosecutor Hubert Jobski said the two men had "in the end trapped themselves in their own web of lies".
Graf showed no emotion as he left the court and declined to comment. His daughter is currently contesting the Australian Open in Melbourne, where she is favourite to win.
"We will object to these sentence requests on Friday," Graf's lawyer Franz Salditt told journalists.
The two men's trial, which began last September, has attracted huge media interest.
Schoepf said Graf and Eckardt were guilty of one count of serious evasion, which she said they had attempted to repeat, and five counts of simple tax evasion.
Lawyers representing Graf and Eckardt will make their closing statements on Friday and Monday.
The court, under German procedure, must then decide on a verdict and, if the verdict is guilty, a sentence. The verdict is expected on January 24 -- just hours before the women's final in Australia.
Steffi Graf herself remains under investigation in the affair but investigators have said suspicions against her are not as serious as those against her father.
She has said she knew little about her financial affairs, entrusting them to her father from the start of a career which has taken her to the pinnacle of women's tennis.
